Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

A German painter paints a Spanish dancer

Describe

Look at the shawl, the ruffles, the pose and the brushwork. What does the painter make move, and what stays still?

Production

Max Slevogt painted La Argentina in 1926. She was born in Buenos Aires and danced Spanish dance on international stages. Who chose the costume and the pose?

Critical

What does this painting present as “Spanish” — and who decided that?

Image: Max Slevogt’s painting of La Argentina standing hands on hips, a pale shawl embroidered with large pink and green flowers over a ruffled dress.

Slevogt La Argentina · Max Slevogt · Public domain · Source

  • Model the first block aloud; pairs do the rest.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

A reference travels without its history

When a dance, a pose or a costume moves to a new country or market, the people who made it can be left behind. Even a performer's face could be sold on a cigarette card.

Image: An 1888 cigarette card: Loïe Fuller, then a stage actress, in breeches and a patterned jacket, with a pug at her feet; printed name “Loie Fuller” and “Virginia Brights Cigarettes”.

Loie Fuller, from the Actors and Actresses series (N45, Type 1) for Virginia Brights Cigarettes MET DP830450 · Allen & Ginter · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Ask of every reference: who is named, who is paid, who is displaced?

How do we know a movement travelled?

  • Rung 1 needs only eyes; rung 4 needs testimony, dates and works.
  • Climb only as high as your evidence.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Madrid → Tokyo

The Japanese dancer Kazuo Ohno saw La Argentina dance as a young man and, about fifty years later, named a solo after her: Admiring La Argentina, 1977.

Watch Admiring La Argentina at source

The title is a quotation you can check. The year he saw her is not settled: archives give 1926, 1927 and 1929.

Image: Caricature of La Argentina on a 1918 Madrid magazine cover: a smiling face with arched brows, sleek dark hair and a zigzag-patterned collar.

1918-12-01, La Novela Teatral, Antonia Mercé (La Argentina), Tovar · Manuel Tovar Siles · Public domain · Source

  • What does Ohno quote: a costume, a gesture, a feeling?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Pleats, again: influence or analogy?

Fortuny pleated silk in the early twentieth century; Issey Miyake made pleated costumes for William Forsythe's Frankfurt Ballet and then the Pleats Please line in 1993. Looking alike is not evidence of influence.

Image: A pink pleated Delphos gown by Fortuny on a display figure; the fine pleats fall straight to the floor.

Pink Delphos dress by Fortuny, 1920s · Mabalu (photograph); Mariano Fortuny (dress) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • Forsythe and Miyake: 1991 or 1992, sources disagree — a documented exchange (rung 3).
  • Fortuny to Miyake: no record here — only analogy (rung 1).

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Who performs whose culture?

Around 1908 the American dancer Ruth St. Denis presented herself as a Hindu goddess for Western audiences, in a costume that sold an idea of “the East”.

Image: Ruth St. Denis in a jewelled, fringed costume, arms extended, holding small cymbals.

Ruth St. Denis in Radha. (3110871798) · Otto Sarony · Public domain · Source

  • What record would separate influence, exchange and appropriation?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Who is made strange?

The label Matières Fécales, founded in Montreal in 2014, built its name on disgust — and in 2026 dressed the actress Sarah Paulson for the Met Gala.

Open the label's Depop shop

Critique, or a new kind of luxury? Answer with evidence — statements, reception, who wore it — not adjectives.

Image: Sarah Paulson on mossy museum steps in a voluminous grey tulle gown with a feathered bodice.

Guests at the 2026 Met Gala 354 · SWinxy (photograph); Matières Fécales (gown) · CC BY 4.0 · Source

  • Abjection is a theory of who is pushed out, not a word for “shocking”.
  • Delfín and Locking: discuss only with evidence.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Butoh has histories, not one look

Butoh began in post-war Japan and travelled to Mexico, Argentina and many other places. White paint is the easiest thing to copy and the least informative.

A pose alone cannot tell us where a movement came from.

Image: Sankai Juku dancers with whitened bodies crouch on a dark stage; three robed figures stand behind.

Sankai Juku · Carlos de las Piedras · CC BY 2.0 · Source

  • Who can name a tradition, and who earns from its circulation?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Recall check

Alone, from memory, three minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Which rung is “it looks like” on the evidence ladder?
  2. Whose name is in the title of Kazuo Ohno's 1977 solo?
  3. Which years do archives give for when Ohno saw her?
  4. What product came after Miyake's pleated ballet costumes?
  5. Which dance began in post-war Japan with Hijikata and Ohno?

Course geometric background · threshold · #c378606cc29b · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • Visual analogy: it only looks alike.
  • Antonia Mercé, La Argentina.
  • 1926, 1927 or 1929: sources disagree.
  • The Pleats Please line, 1993.
  • Butoh.

Exercise 1 · Transform your capture

Choose one: widen a vertical photo to cinema format, extend a sleeve or hem with Generative Fill, restyle the garment in Firefly, or animate a still into five seconds of video.

All four prompts in the lesson

Keep the original and the transformed image side by side, and mark what the AI invented.

Exercise 2 · Audit what the machine assumes

Ask Firefly for four images of a “butoh dancer” or a “flamenco dancer”, list what the model assumes, and decide which rung of the evidence ladder a generated image can reach.

extensive acts of appropriation

(Mejias and Couldry 2024, introduction)

Audit prompt in the lesson

Write your audit sentences and a two-line AI declaration: the tool, what it contributed, and what you checked.

Image: Antonia Mercé, La Argentina, in 1913: one arm raised with castanets, in a long embroidered dress, photographed in a Madrid magazine.

Antonia Mercé · Unknown photographer (Mundo Gráfico, 1913) · Public domain · Source

  • A generated image can only resemble: rung 1.
  • Declaration → /ai-declaration/.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 3 of 3

Carry forward

Climb only as high as your evidence, and ask who is credited, paid or displaced when a movement travels. A generated image can resemble a tradition; it cannot document one.
